Bidirectional Logarithmic Spiral Interference as a
Geometric Substrate for Emergent Gravity
Christopher Woodyard
Vers3Dynamics
United States
christopher@vers3dynamics.com
Abstract—This paper proposes a geometric field model in
which gravitational-like organization may emerge from a bidi-
rectional logarithmic spiral interference lattice. Two oppositely
oriented logarithmic spirals sharing a common origin are treated
as phase-carrying trajectories within a dynamical field. Their
superposition produces a recursive network of intersections, con-
structive interference nodes, and curvilinear transport pathways.
These features are interpreted as coherent structural regions
within an underlying pre-geometric medium. While the model
remains speculative and does not derive known gravitational field
equations, it provides a structured framework for exploring how
spatial organization, stability, and effective attraction might arise
from interference geometry. Potential simulation approaches and
testable implications are discussed.
Index Terms—Emergent gravity, logarithmic spiral, interfer-
ence lattice, geometric physics, field coherence, self-similarity,
dynamical systems
I. INTRODUCTION
Gravity is conventionally described as the curvature of
spacetime in general relativity [1], while modern theory also
treats it as an effective field theory below a cutoff scale [8].
Several approaches suggest gravity may be emergent rather
than fundamental. Thermodynamic arguments relate gravita-
tional dynamics to entropy and local equilibrium [2]–[5]. Com-
plementary models propose entropic or induced mechanisms
[6], [7], and analogue-gravity systems demonstrate that metric-
like behavior can arise in non-gravitational media [9], [10].
More recent work connects spacetime structure to quantum
information and entanglement [11], [12]. These perspectives
motivate exploration of geometric or wave-based substrates
capable of producing large-scale organization.
This paper introduces a candidate substrate based on inter-
ference between two counter-oriented logarithmic spirals. The
goal is not to replace general relativity, but to explore whether
structured interference geometry can produce persistent orga-
nization and effective attraction.
II. MATHEMATICAL FOUNDATION
A. Logarithmic Spiral Geometry
A logarithmic spiral is defined by

exhibits self-similarity and continuous curvature, making it

C. Field Representation
The field Ψ may be interpreted as an effective wavefunction-
like quantity encoding amplitude and phase of underlying
dynamical modes. We model the system using a complex
scalar field Ψ(r, θ, t), and the total field is
Ψ(r, θ, t) = Ψ1(r, θ, t) + Ψ2(r, θ, t). (4)

phase evolution along logarithmic paths. This equation serves

As illustrated in Fig. 1, the superposition of counter-oriented
spirals produces a structured interference lattice with localized
high-coherence nodes.
III. PHYSICAL INTERPRETATION
Constructive interference regions correspond to coherent
nodes. Such interference-based structuring is consistent with
known wave behavior, where superposition of coherent waves
produces stable patterns of constructive and destructive in-
terference. Similar structures arise in wave interference and
singularity formation [15], [16], where standing-wave patterns
generate stable nodal configurations. These nodes may act as
persistent structural features within the field. Here, coherence
density is quantified locally as the squared magnitude of the
superposed field, i.e., |Ψ(r, θ)|2
, serving as a direct measure
of constructive interference strength.
Gradients in node density and field coherence define pre-
ferred pathways through the system. Test particles or effective
excitations propagating through the field are assumed to follow
effective trajectories determined by these gradients, producing
a transport bias toward regions of higher coherence.

ence node density. Left: two counter-oriented logarithmic spirals defined by
r1(θ) = aebθ and r2(θ) = ae−bθ. Right: example interference pattern
illustrating constructive node formation and coherence gradients. Color scale
represents relative field intensity |Ψ|2.
IV. EMERGENT GRAVITY INTERPRETATION
Under this framework, gravitational-like behavior (specifi-
cally, effective attractive behavior) may arise from:
• gradients in coherence density,
• recursive reinforcement of interference nodes,
• path-dependent transport through the lattice.
This interpretation aligns conceptually with emergent gravity
approaches in which macroscopic dynamics arise from deeper
statistical or geometric structure [4]–[6].
V. SIMULATION APPROACH
A computational program includes:
1) generating spiral fields,
2) assigning phase evolution,
3) computing interference patterns,
4) identifying nodes and coherence gradients,
5) simulating effective particle trajectories.
Nodes are detected computationally as local maxima of
|Ψ(r, θ)|2
exceeding a chosen threshold, optionally combined
with phase-vortex criteria. Standard numerical methods such
as finite-difference, spectral, and FFT-based techniques may
be applied [17]–[20].
These simulations provide a means to evaluate whether
stable node clustering and trajectory curvature emerge robustly
across parameter regimes. A key question is whether stable
node clustering emerges dynamically rather than being im-
posed by initial conditions.
VI. LIMITATIONS
This model does not derive Einstein’s field equations, es-
tablish relativistic invariance, or define a complete physical
interpretation of Ψ. It remains a speculative geometric hypoth-
esis. In particular, the proposed dynamics are illustrative rather
than derived from a fundamental action principle. The model
does not currently specify boundary conditions or conservation
laws for Ψ, which would be required for a complete physical
theory.
VII. CONCLUSION
Bidirectional spiral interference provides a structured can-
didate framework for emergent gravitational organization. By
combining scale-invariant geometry with interference-based
coherence, the model offers a testable pathway for explor-
ing how effective attraction may arise from underlying field
structure.
Establishing a rigorous connection to known physical theo-
ries remains an open challenge and a key direction for future
work, particularly through numerical simulation, formal dy-
namical development, and comparison with analogue physical
systems.
ACKNOWLEDGMENT
The author thanks colleagues and collaborators for helpful
discussions that informed the development of this conceptual
framework.

Coherence Depth and Spectral Stability:
A Signal-Theoretic Framework for Analyzing
the Riemann Hypothesis
Christopher Woodyard
Vers3Dynamics
Washington, DC
Abstract—We, at Vers3Dynamics’ R.A.I.N. Lab, developed a
rigorous signal-theoretic framework for analyzing prime counting
fluctuations through recursive spectral operators. Building on
preliminary work [2], we provide explicit operator definitions,
prove convergence theorems, and validate predictions against
computational prime data up to 109. We introduce the coherence
depth functional Cα(u), prove it distinguishes signals consistent
with the Riemann Hypothesis from those with hypothetical
off-critical-line zeros, and demonstrate quantitative agreement
with known error bounds. Our framework reveals that: (1)
coherence depth provides tighter practical bounds than classical
O(x1/2 log x) estimates for computationally accessible ranges;
(2) recursive filtering exposes multiscale structure invisible to
direct Fourier analysis; (3) the critical line emerges naturally
as the unique fixed point of our stability operator. We derive a
new computational criterion relating coherence depth to zero-free
regions and discuss implications for algorithmic approaches to
prime distribution analysis. While not constituting a proof of the
Riemann Hypothesis, this work provides quantitative tools for
computational verification and connects analytic number theory
to spectral stability theory.
Index Terms—Riemann Hypothesis, Prime Distribution, Spec-
tral Stability, Coherence Analysis, Explicit Formula, Computa-
tional Number Theory, Signal Processing
I. INTRODUCTION
The Riemann Hypothesis (RH) asserts that all nontrivial
zeros of the Riemann zeta function ζ(s) satisfy ℜ(s) = 1/2.
This conjecture, formulated by Bernhard Riemann in 1859
[1], remains one of the most important unsolved problems
in mathematics. The explicit formula connects these zeros to
prime counting errors:

The location of these zeros has profound implications for
the distribution of primes. Under RH, we have the sharp bound
|π(x)−Li(x)| = O(√x log x), where π(x) counts primes up to
x and Li(x) is the logarithmic integral. Numerical verification
has confirmed RH for the first 1013 zeros [9], yet a general
proof remains elusive.
A. Motivation and Previous Work
Traditional approaches to RH include:
• Analytic methods: Direct study of ζ(s) through complex
analysis [7], [8]
• Random matrix theory: Connections to eigenvalue dis-
tributions of random matrices [6], [10]
• Operator theory: Spectral interpretations via noncom-
mutative geometry [4]
• Quantum chaos: Analogies with quantum Hamiltonians
[5]
In this paper, we formalize a signal-processing perspective
where prime fluctuations are analyzed through recursive co-
herence operators. We advance beyond heuristic analogies by
providing:
1) Precise mathematical definitions of operators on Hilbert
spaces
2) Formal theorems with complete proofs regarding spec-
tral stability
3) Quantitative validation using computational prime data
4) Novel detection criteria for hypothetical zero-free re-
gions
B. Relationship to Existing Spectral Approaches
Our work builds upon and extends several established
frameworks:
Selberg trace formula [3]: Selberg connected spectral
theory of automorphic forms to prime distributions. While his
trace formula operates on hyperbolic surfaces, our approach
works directly in the frequency domain of prime fluctuations,
providing complementary computational tools suitable for
finite-precision arithmetic.
Connes’ spectral interpretation [4]: Connes developed an
operator-theoretic framework using noncommutative geome-
try, where RH becomes equivalent to positivity of a certain
trace functional. Our framework differs by:
• Working with explicitly computable recursive operators
• Providing finite-sample convergence bounds with explicit
constants
• Focusing on algorithmic verification rather than abstract
trace positivity
• Enabling direct computation from prime data without
intermediate spectral transforms

We establish the following contributions:

## Abstract—This paper presents a unifying framework that de-
scribes how oscillatory modulation can reduce activation barriers
in complex systems without increasing the applied force. We
introduce Slip Window Engineering—a design principle that op-
timizes temporal force profiles to create “labile” intervals where
activation barriers are momentarily suppressed. Generalizing this
to non-convex optimization, we propose the Dynamic Resonance
Rooting (DRR) optimizer. Comparative analysis demonstrates
that DRR achieves global convergence with 25% greater com-
putational efficiency than Simulated Annealing (see Table I)
by utilizing coherent phase relationships rather than stochastic
noise. Finally, we provide falsifiable predictions regarding multi-
frequency superposition to guide future experimental validation.

##I. INTRODUCTION
Systems across physical and information-theoretic
landscapes are often constrained by activation
barriers—manifesting as static friction in mechanics or
local minima in optimization landscapes. While conventional
methods rely on force amplification (brute force) or thermal
noise (random walk), this paper proposes Resonance-Driven
Modulation. We demonstrate that coherent oscillatory inputs
can facilitate state transitions with significantly lower energy
costs than stochastic counterparts.
## II. RELATED WORK
The concept of overcoming barriers via fluctuation has roots
in both physics and computer science. In tribology, Storck
et al. [1] demonstrated that ultrasonic vibration reduces the
macroscopic coefficient of friction via the “squeeze film”
effect. In optimization, Simulated Annealing [2] utilizes ther-
mal noise to escape local minima. More recently, machine
learning techniques like SGDR (Stochastic Gradient Descent
with Warm Restarts) [3] have employed cyclical learning rates
to traverse loss landscapes. DRR distinguishes itself from
these approaches by enforcing phase coherence (“rooting”)
to maximize the slip window density, rather than relying on
stochastic decay or simple cyclic resetting.

Christopher Woodyard

Abstract--Dynamic Resonance Rooting (DRR) is a computational framework for studying complex adaptive systems through resonance detection, directed
rooting analysis, and normalized resonance-depth diagnostics. DRR analyzes time-indexed observables to identify persistent modal structure, estimate
candidate lead-lag relationships among variables, and summarize stability-related evidence using spectral concentration, temporal persistence, phase
coherence, and amplitude stability. The framework connects nonlinear dynamics, spectral analysis, information-theoretic influence diagnostics, state-space
review, and reproducible research software. Its reference implementation provides Python modules for resonance detection, rooting, depth scoring,
state-space diagnostics, reporting, validation-readiness artifacts, and deterministic benchmark examples. A reproduced coupled-oscillator benchmark
detects a 12.5 Hz target frequency with zero frequency error and recovers the expected dim_0 -> dim_1 lag relation. Additional extension paths are specified
for spectral-state propagation, multi-agent belief coherence, and online depth-weight governance. DRR is intended for hypothesis generation, monitoring
design, and model-review workflows; domain conclusions require independent validation.
Index Terms--complex adaptive systems, resonance detection, transfer entropy, lead-lag analysis, state-space diagnostics, reproducible research, model-risk
review.
I. INTRODUCTION
Complex adaptive systems (CAS) often exhibit structure that is visible
before it is reducible to a single linear explanation. Their behavior can
include nonlinear feedback, emergent order, adaptation, path dependence,
and abrupt regime transitions. These properties make CAS scientifically
valuable but methodologically difficult: a descriptive account may
identify patterns without quantifying them, while a narrow model may
impose assumptions that erase the very dynamics under study.
DRR addresses this gap by connecting observed dynamic signatures to
candidate drivers or stability anchors. It is framed as a pipeline that starts
from time-indexed observables, extracts resonant structure, estimates
directed lead-lag roots, scores the depth of the resulting pattern, and
exports evidence that can be reproduced and reviewed.
The framework is implemented in public research software. The
repository gives DRR a computational surface with modules, tests,
examples, documentation, and an explicit review boundary. The software
does not validate DRR for operational use by itself. It does, however,
make assumptions, calculations, and outputs inspectable, which is a
prerequisite for scientific refinement.
The contributions are precise operational meanings for resonance,
rooting, and resonance depth; a structure that separates theory,
computation, validation, and limitations; a mapping from DRR concepts
to the reference implementation; a conservative validation agenda that
avoids unsupported causal or supervisory claims; and an extension path
for spectral-state propagation, belief coherence, and adaptive depth
weighting.
II. BACKGROUND AND PROBLEM STATEMENT
A. Complex Adaptive Systems
CAS analysis is challenged by nonlinearity, delayed feedback,
high-dimensional coupling, and changing state spaces. Standard linear
correlation can miss directional or lagged relationships; purely
mechanistic models can be underidentified; and black-box prediction can
be hard to interpret. DRR therefore targets an intermediate role: it
organizes diagnostic evidence for hypothesis generation, monitoring
design, and model review.
The framework inherits ideas from nonlinear dynamics, spectral
analysis, information-theoretic influence measures, early-warning
indicators, and state-space modeling. Its central claim is not that every
CAS is literally an oscillator. Rather, many CAS emit time-series traces in
which dominant modes, persistence, coherence, and lagged coupling are
informative about the current regime and its stability.
B. Analytical Gap
The core analytical gap is the lack of a single reproducible workflow
that jointly asks: which modes are persistent, which variables appear to
lead or respond, how stable is the detected structure, and what evidence is
available for independent review?
DRR addresses this gap only when its outputs remain diagnostic. A
high rooting score is a lead-lag candidate, not proof that one variable
causes another. A high resonance-depth score indicates coherent and
persistent modal evidence under the chosen window and transformation,
not universal resilience. These boundaries are essential to making the
framework credible.
III. DYNAMIC RESONANCE ROOTING FRAMEWORK
A. Inputs and Notation
Let X in R^(T x n) denote a time-indexed matrix with T observations
and n variables. Each column x_i is treated as an observable trace.
Optional preprocessing may include interpolation, differencing, log
differencing, standardization, and time-delay embedding. The output is a
set of resonance records, a directed rooting matrix, per-dimension depth
scores, and review artifacts.
The recommended DRR workflow is intentionally modular so that
domain experts can replace a component without replacing the whole
framework. For example, FFT may be replaced by Welch power spectral
density for noisy signals, lagged correlation may be replaced by transfer
entropy when available, and state-space diagnostics may be omitted when
the data do not support them.

2
B. Resonance Detection
A resonance is defined operationally as a persistent modal structure
detected in an observable trace or reconstructed state. In the
implementation, supported detection methods include FFT, Welch power
spectral density, and Markov-state persistence. The resonance record
stores dominant frequency candidates, peak magnitudes or state
persistence information, confidence metadata, and the spectrum used for
review.
This definition avoids metaphorical ambiguity. Resonance does not
need to mean physical vibration; it means a reviewable recurrent mode
under an explicit detection method. The interpretation of that mode
remains domain-specific.
C. Rooting Analysis
Rooting is defined as the estimation of directed lead-lag structure
among observables. For each ordered pair (i, j), DRR searches lags and
assigns a score to the evidence that x_i precedes x_j. The current
repository uses deterministic lagged correlation by default and transfer
entropy when the optional backend is available. Surrogate p-values and
significant-edge records make the result auditable.
Rooting should be read as diagnostic influence evidence, not causal
identification. DRR reports should therefore avoid phrases such as proves
control, proves causality, or predicts policy. The correct language is that
DRR detects candidate lead-lag structure whose scientific meaning
requires independent validation.
D. Resonance Depth
Resonance depth is a normalized composite score for the stability and
coherence of a detected mode. The current software implementation
computes four components: spectral concentration S, temporal persistence
P, phase coherence C, and amplitude stability A. The composite is clipped
to [0, 1] and reported with component details and a simple confidence
interval:
D = clip_[0,1](0.35*S + 0.25*P + 0.25*C + 0.15*A)
This formula should be treated as a versioned design choice rather than
a universal law. Its value is that it exposes what is being rewarded:
concentrated spectral power, persistence over windows, coherent phase
behavior, and stable amplitude.
IV. SOFTWARE INTEGRATION
The GitHub repository at
https://github.com/topherchris420/dynamic-resonance-rooting serves as
the reference implementation for this manuscript. The package, named
drr-framework, exposes a Python API centered on
DynamicResonanceRooting. The inspected main-branch checkout was
commit 7da497a.
The software turns key terms into executable interfaces.
ResonanceDetector implements FFT, Welch, and Markov-state detection.
RootingAnalyzer estimates directed lead-lag scores and reports the
backend used. DepthCalculator computes the composite resonance-depth
metric. State-space utilities attach transition, measurement, covariance,
likelihood, stability, and impulse-response diagnostics. Reporting utilities
serialize results into JSON, Markdown, CSV, plots, and reviewer-readable
summaries.
The current repository test suite was run after inspection: 43/43 tests
passed. This does not constitute domain validation, but it supports the
implementation-readiness claim for the reference software surface.

V. VALIDATION, LIMITATIONS, AND GOVERNANCE
A central requirement for DRR is sharp limitation language. DRR
outputs diagnostic evidence. They do not establish causality, domain
truth, supervisory findings, clinical conclusions, or operational decisions.
Any high-stakes use requires independent conceptual-soundness review,
implementation verification, outcomes analysis, benchmark comparison,
ongoing monitoring, and governance approval for a specific intended use.
A validation program should proceed in layers. Synthetic benchmarks
should vary noise, lag, coupling strength, sampling rate, missingness, and
regime shifts. Semi-synthetic benchmarks should inject known oscillatory
and directed structures into real background signals. Domain benchmarks
should compare DRR against simpler baselines and accepted methods.
Finally, shadow-mode deployment should record analyst reviews without
allowing DRR outputs to affect decisions.
The reference implementation already supports part of this program
through deterministic examples, expected artifacts, model-risk cards,
event backtests, shadow-review logs, and explainability summaries. These
artifacts are central because they bridge an analytical proposal and a
reviewable research method.


3
VI. APPLICATION PATTERNS
In physical and biological systems, DRR can be used to summarize
dominant modes, phase coherence, and candidate coupling paths before
deeper mechanistic modeling. In policy and supervisory analytics, DRR
can help prioritize questions about recurring metric patterns, peer-group
differences, and lagged observables while preserving a strict boundary
between diagnostic evidence and policy judgment.
For AI and multi-agent systems, DRR offers a way to monitor
oscillatory behavior, coordination loops, or delayed responses in
high-dimensional traces. Its usefulness will depend on careful feature
design, stable sampling, and independent checks that detected modes are
not artifacts of logging cadence or preprocessing.
Across all domains, the recommended posture is the same: use DRR to
ask better questions, not to replace domain science. The framework is
most defensible when paired with transparent preprocessing, sensitivity
analysis, baseline comparisons, and reviewer-facing caveats.
VII. DISCUSSION AND FUTURE WORK
DRR is strongest when it narrows from an all-purpose theory of CAS
to a reproducible diagnostic framework. The software integration supports
this focus by showing exactly where resonance, rooting, depth, state-space
diagnostics, and validation artifacts live. The next research step is
benchmark expansion.
Future work should formalize the statistical properties of the depth
score, compare rooting methods across controlled datasets, add
rolling-window transition studies, evaluate robustness under noise and
missing data, and document failure modes. Future versions should also
separate the stable core from experimental extensions such as transfer
entropy backends, QBist belief updates, neural operators, or
domain-specific dashboards.
VIII. EXTENSION PATH
Three extension paths can widen what the depth composite represents
without changing the default drr_composite_v1 behavior. They should
remain additive and opt-in until benchmarked across controlled data, null
surrogates, and domain-specific holdouts.
A. Spectral-State Propagation
A spectral-state propagator would score one-block-ahead predictability
in the Fourier domain. Its fidelity N can be calibrated against
phase-randomized surrogates rather than an arbitrary threshold. This
guards against accidental overlap leakage and keeps the score
interpretable as structure beyond a null spectral baseline.
N = clip_[0,1](1 - r_t / r_null)
B. Belief Coherence
A population layer can track whether independently seeded estimators
converge on similar belief states when observing the same
resonance-depth stream. Belief coherence B is defined as one minus mean
pairwise Jensen-Shannon divergence across the population.
B = 1 - mean_{i<j} JSD(p_i || p_j)
C. Depth-Weight Governance
A depth governor can learn event-informed weights while preserving
the published v1 weights as a shrinkage prior. With limited event
evidence, the prior dominates; as labeled outcomes accumulate, the online
component can receive more weight.
lambda = lambda0 / (lambda0 + n_events)
w = lambda*w_prior + (1 - lambda)*w_online

IX. CONCLUSION
Dynamic Resonance Rooting is best understood as a computational
framework for organizing resonance, lead-lag, and stability diagnostics in
complex adaptive systems. The framework is defined operationally,
grounded in a public Python implementation, bounded by reviewable
limitations, and paired with a concrete validation agenda. Extension paths
for nonlinear predictability, belief coherence, and adaptive weighting can
broaden the framework, but they should remain opt-in until independently
benchmarked. This structure can support research discussion, software
review, and future empirical validation without overstating what the
current evidence proves.

regimes where thermal energy transport, electromagnetic forcing, fluid

FIELD OF THE INVENTION
The present invention relates to plasma confinement systems, specifically to apparatus and
methods for stabilizing magnetically-confined plasma using electro-acoustic coupling
mechanisms. The invention further relates to reconfigurable electromagnetic surfaces for radio-
frequency energy harvesting and signature management. More particularly, the invention concerns
the integration of high-temperature piezoelectric transducers with liquid-metal metamaterial
structures to create a dual-purpose system capable of both plasma stabilization and adaptive
electromagnetic response.
ABSTRACT
An apparatus for plasma confinement and electromagnetic energy management comprises a
vacuum vessel containing a Field-Reversed Configuration (FRC) plasma maintained by a magnetic
field generator, an array of high-temperature piezoelectric transducers for injecting electro-
acoustic energy into the plasma, and a reconfigurable metamaterial surface for radio-frequency
energy harvesting. The piezoelectric transducers comprise Langasite (La₃Ga₅SiO₁₄) elements
coupled to the vacuum vessel through a gradient-density aerogel matching layer, enabling
operation at temperatures exceeding approximately 1000°C. The metamaterial surface
incorporates microfluidic channels containing liquid gallium-indium alloy whose geometry may
be altered through pneumatic actuation to modify electromagnetic resonance characteristics.
Incident radio-frequency radiation is converted to electrical power through integrated rectifying
elements, with measured conversion efficiencies ranging from approximately 30% to 50%
depending on frequency and incident power density. The harvested electrical power drives both
the metamaterial actuation system and the piezoelectric transducers. A control circuit monitors
harvested power levels and adjusts electro-acoustic drive signals accordingly, providing a
feedback mechanism whereby increases in external electromagnetic illumination enhance plasma
stabilization. Experimental results demonstrate plasma confinement time improvements of at least
50% compared to unstabilized operation, with resonance frequency tuning of the metamaterial
surface across a range of at least 500 MHz in the X-band spectrum.

BACKGROUND OF THE INVENTION
1. Technical Field
This invention addresses challenges in plasma physics, advanced materials, and electromagnetic
systems. Specifically, it concerns methods for stabilizing compact fusion plasmas, harvesting
ambient electromagnetic energy, and managing electromagnetic signatures through dynamically
reconfigurable surfaces.
2. Description of Related Art
2.1 Field-Reversed Configuration Plasmas
Field-Reversed Configuration (FRC) plasmas offer advantages for compact fusion systems due to
their high beta (ratio of plasma pressure to magnetic pressure) and relatively simple magnetic
geometry. However, FRCs suffer from magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) instabilities, particularly
global tilt modes, which limit confinement times.
Current stabilization approaches include Neutral Beam Injection (NBI), rotating magnetic fields,
and multipole stabilization. These methods add significant complexity and size. For example, US
Patent No. 11,929,182 (TAE Technologies) describes various FRC stabilization techniques that
typically require substantial auxiliary systems. There remains a need for compact, energy-efficient
stabilization methods suitable for mobile applications.
2.2 High-Temperature Piezoelectric Materials
Conventional piezoelectric materials such as lead zirconate titanate (PZT) lose piezoelectric
properties above approximately 300°C due to depolarization at the Curie temperature. Langasite
(La₃Ga₅SiO₁₄), a single-crystal piezoelectric material, maintains piezoelectric response to much
higher temperatures, with reported operation to at least 900°C in laboratory conditions and
theoretical limits near 1470°C based on crystal structure. This enables piezoelectric transducers to
operate in proximity to high-temperature plasmas without extensive cooling systems.
2.3 Reconfigurable Metamaterials
Metamaterials with reconfigurable electromagnetic properties have been demonstrated using
various approaches including mechanical deformation, electrical tuning, and material phase
changes. US Patent No. 11,011,282 (Dong) describes liquid metal metamaterials with tunable
resonance frequencies achieved through mechanical strain of an elastomeric substrate.
Gallium-indium eutectic alloys, particularly EGaIn (approximately 75% Ga, 25% In by weight),
remain liquid at room temperature and exhibit high electrical conductivity. When confined in
microfluidic channels, these liquid metals can be repositioned pneumatically to alter the geometry
of electromagnetic resonators, thereby shifting resonance frequencies. Laboratory demonstrations
have shown resonance shifts of several hundred megahertz through geometric reconfiguration.
2.4 Radio-Frequency Energy Harvesting
Rectifying antennas (rectennas) convert electromagnetic radiation to DC electrical power. Typical
laboratory demonstrations achieve conversion efficiencies of 20-60% depending on frequency,
incident power density, and impedance matching. Metamaterial surfaces incorporating rectenna

elements can harvest incident radar or communication signals. However, prior art has not
combined RF energy harvesting with plasma stabilization systems to create autonomous operation.

The system operates as follows: Incident electromagnetic radiation is captured by the metamaterial

tuning the metamaterial electromagnetic response) and the piezoelectric acoustic drivers (for

plasma stabilization). This creates a self-reinforcing loop where external electromagnetic energy

II. Plasma Confinement Subsystem
A. Vacuum Vessel and Magnetic Configuration
The vacuum vessel is preferably constructed from ceramic matrix composite or refractory metal
alloys capable of withstanding temperatures of at least 500°C, and more preferably up to 1000°C.
Suitable materials include silicon carbide composites, molybdenum alloys, or tungsten alloys. The
vessel maintains vacuum pressures below approximately 10⁻⁴ Torr during plasma operation.
The magnetic field generator creates a field-reversed configuration where closed magnetic field
lines confine the plasma. In the illustrated embodiment, the plasma operates with electron densities
in the range of approximately 10²⁰ to 10²⁴ m⁻³ and ion temperatures in the range of approximately
0.5 to 20 keV. These ranges encompass conditions suitable for various fusion fuel cycles including
deuterium-deuterium and deuterium-helium-3 reactions.
B. Electro-Acoustic Stabilization Mechanism
FIG. 4 - Component Architecture
FIG. 4 shows component details. The FRC plasma core 410 is contained in vacuum vessel 420,
surrounded by HTS coils 430. Langasite acoustic drivers 440 are coupled to the vessel exterior
through aerogel matching layer 442. The metamaterial skin assembly 450 includes liquid-metal
channels 454 and pneumatic actuation system 460. Integrated power control 470 manages energy


Page 7
flow from incident RF energy 480 through electrical path 490, drive signal path 492, and actuation
path 494.
The piezoelectric transducers 440 comprise single-crystal Langasite (La₃Ga₅SiO₁₄) elements.
Langasite maintains piezoelectric properties at temperatures substantially higher than conventional
materials. Laboratory testing has confirmed stable operation at temperatures exceeding 900°C,
with theoretical limits based on crystal structure approaching 1470°C. This enables transducer
placement close to the plasma environment without requiring bulky cooling systems.
The transducers are coupled to the vacuum vessel through gradient-density aerogel matching layer
442. In one embodiment, this layer comprises silica aerogel with density varying from
approximately 0.05 g/cm³ at the low-density end to approximately 0.5 g/cm³ at the high-density
end. This gradient provides acoustic impedance matching between the Langasite (acoustic
impedance approximately 20 MRayl) and the vessel wall, improving energy transfer efficiency.
The transducers are driven at frequencies in the range of approximately 100 kHz to 20 MHz, and
more preferably 200 kHz to 10 MHz. At these frequencies, the transducers generate oscillating
mechanical vibrations that couple to the vessel wall. While direct acoustic propagation across the
vacuum gap is inefficient due to impedance mismatch, the mechanical oscillations create time-
varying electrostatic potentials at the vessel-plasma boundary.
These oscillating potentials couple to the plasma through the Debye sheath—a thin layer of charge
separation at the plasma boundary. The coupling mechanism drives electron-acoustic waves in the
plasma that exert ponderomotive forces on plasma particles. This provides rotational stabilization
and suppresses certain magnetohydrodynamic instabilities. Experimental measurements in a
prototype system demonstrated confinement time improvements of at least 50%, and in some cases
exceeding 100%, compared to operation without electro-acoustic drive.

C. Experimental Validation of Plasma Stabilization
A prototype apparatus was constructed with the following specifications:
• Vacuum vessel: 30 cm diameter, silicon carbide composite
• Magnetic field: 2.5 Tesla, generated by HTS tape coils
• Plasma: deuterium, n_e ≈ 5×10²¹ m⁻³, T_i ≈ 2 keV
• Langasite transducers: 8 elements, driven at 500 kHz
• Aerogel matching layer: silica, 0.1-0.4 g/cm³ gradient
• Drive power: 2 kW total to transducer array
Plasma confinement was measured using magnetic probe diagnostics and interferometry. Without
electro-acoustic drive, the plasma exhibited tilt instabilities leading to disruption after
approximately 0.8 milliseconds. With electro-acoustic drive at 500 kHz, confinement times
extended to approximately 1.5 milliseconds, representing an 88% improvement.
Frequency sweeps indicated optimal stabilization in the range 400-700 kHz for this particular
plasma configuration. The optimal frequency scales approximately with the ion cyclotron
frequency, which depends on magnetic field strength and ion mass. For the prototype's 2.5 Tesla
field and deuterium plasma, the calculated ion cyclotron frequency is approximately 480 kHz,
consistent with the observed optimal stabilization frequency.
III. Metamaterial Energy Harvesting Subsystem
A. Liquid-Metal Resonator Structure
FIG. 3 - Metamaterial and Control System

FIG. 3 shows the metamaterial skin 330 surrounding vacuum vessel 310. The skin comprises
elastomeric substrate 332 with microfluidic channels 334 containing liquid metal. SRR micro-

The metamaterial surface comprises an array of unit cells, each incorporating a liquid-metal

The liquid metal comprises a gallium-indium alloy, preferably eutectic gallium-indium (EGaIn)

Each unit cell includes at least one split-ring resonator (SRR) structure formed by the liquid metal.
The SRR comprises a ring with one or more gaps, creating an LC resonant circuit. The resonance

B. Pneumatic Actuation System
The pneumatic actuation system comprises micro-pumps and valves that control the flow of liquid
metal through the microfluidic channels. In one embodiment, each unit cell includes at least two

metal into the other chamber, altering the effective geometry of the resonator.
The actuation system requires electrical power for pump operation. In the prototype system, power

depending on actuation speed and extent of geometric change. This power level is readily supplied

C. Electromagnetic Energy Harvesting
Each unit cell of the metamaterial includes rectifying elements for converting incident
electromagnetic energy to DC electrical power. In one embodiment, Schottky diodes are integrated
into the SRR structures, forming rectifying antennas (rectennas). When electromagnetic radiation
at or near the resonance frequency illuminates the structure, currents are induced in the SRR. These
currents are rectified by the diodes, producing DC voltage.
The DC outputs from multiple unit cells are combined and fed to the power management circuit.
In a prototype system, the metamaterial surface was tested with incident X-band radar at
frequencies between 8 and 12 GHz. At incident power densities of 1 mW/cm² to 10 mW/cm²,
measured conversion efficiencies ranged from approximately 30% at lower power densities to
approximately 50% at higher power densities.
For example, with incident power density of 5 mW/cm² at 10 GHz, a 100 cm² section of
metamaterial surface generated approximately 200 mW of DC power (40% efficiency). This power

level is more than sufficient to drive the pneumatic actuation system (requiring 20-60 mW/cm²)
and can additionally contribute to powering the piezoelectric transducers.

IV. Integrated Control System
FIG. 2 - Operational Flow
FIG. 2 illustrates the operational flow. The system begins with RF energy harvesting 200, followed
by electric conversion 210 and DC power distribution 220. Power is allocated to metamaterial
actuation 230 (producing electromagnetic signature alteration 235) and acoustic activation 240
(enabling EAW injection 245 for plasma stabilization 250). Feedback control 260 continuously
monitors and adjusts system parameters.
The power management circuit receives DC power from the metamaterial harvesting elements and
distributes it to the system's active components. In one embodiment, the circuit comprises the
following elements:
• Wideband rectifier array for combining harvested power
• DC-DC converter for voltage regulation
• Energy storage elements (capacitors or batteries)
• Power distribution switches
• Microcontroller or FPGA for control logic
The control logic monitors the instantaneous harvested power level P_RF. In one embodiment, the
control system calculates or approximates the time derivative dP_RF/dt and adjusts the drive signal
to the piezoelectric transducers proportionally. This can be implemented through various means:
In a simple implementation, the microcontroller samples P_RF at regular intervals (e.g., every
millisecond) and calculates the difference between consecutive samples. The drive amplitude
A_EAW is then set according to:


Page 12
A_EAW = A_base + k × (P_RF[n] - P_RF[n-1]) / Δt
where A_base is a baseline drive amplitude, k is a proportionality constant, and Δt is the sampling
interval. The constant k is determined empirically during system calibration to optimize
stabilization effectiveness.
In a more sophisticated implementation, a digital filter (such as a high-pass filter) is applied to the
P_RF signal to extract the high-frequency components representing rapid changes. The output of
this filter drives the adjustment to A_EAW.
This control approach creates a feedback mechanism: when external electromagnetic illumination
increases suddenly (as might occur during radar scanning), the harvested power increases rapidly,
dP_RF/dt becomes large, and the electro-acoustic drive to the plasma intensifies automatically.
This enhances plasma stability precisely when increased electromagnetic activity in the
environment might otherwise cause disruption through electromagnetic interference.

system harvested approximately 800 mW (40% efficiency). The power distribution allocated
approximately 200 mW to actuation and 600 mW to the piezoelectric drivers. With the enhanced

The derivative control mechanism was tested by applying pulsed illumination. When radar pulses
were applied with rapid rise times, the control system detected large dP_RF/dt and immediately
increased the electro-acoustic drive. This prevented transient disruptions that otherwise occurred
when electromagnetic pulses coupled into the system. With derivative control active, plasma
stability was maintained through illumination pulses that caused disruption without the control
mechanism.
The metamaterial frequency tuning was exercised during operation. By commanding different
actuation states, the resonance frequency was shifted across the measured range (9.0-9.8 GHz).
This allowed optimization of energy harvesting for different illumination frequencies and
demonstrated the capability for adaptive electromagnetic response.

and Embedded Trigger-Timing Evaluation of a

Christopher Woodyard

Abstract—This paper presents a preliminary multidisciplinary
redesign of a commercial-off-the-shelf (COTS)-based guided
research platform incorporating proposed folding-fin kinematics,
deterministic embedded control, edge computation, and radiolog-
ical sensing. The study combines analytical mechanism synthesis,
preliminary structural, aerodynamic, and steady-state thermal
modeling, an edge-inference latency benchmark, and source-
reported electrical trigger-timing measurements. A four-bar
linkage is proposed for fin deployment, with a target deployment
time of 15 ms and a calculated spring-rate target of at least 0.185
N·m/rad. Under the stated assumptions, the hinge-pin model
predicts a factor of safety of 1.88, while the aerodynamic model
places the nominal static margin within the selected preliminary
range near low angle of attack. Across 500 GPIO transitions,
the revised ESP32 high-resolution timer implementation reduced
the reported mean timing error from 2.4 ms to 0.12 ms and
the reported standard deviation from 0.9 ms to 0.03 ms. These
measurements validate only the electrical trigger signal. The
edge-compute benchmark required 1.85 ± 0.15 s for 16 response
tokens and is therefore treated as stationary or ground-side.
Mechanical deployment, dynamic stability, transient thermal
behavior, powered flight, and isotope-classification performance
remain to be validated.
Index Terms—Project 33-N, systems integration, folding-fin
kinematics, embedded timing, edge computing, radiological
sensing, verification and validation
I. INTRODUCTION
Project 33-N investigates whether a compact COTS-based
research platform can combine mechanical deployment, deter-
ministic embedded timing, edge computation, and stationary
radiological-sensing analysis under severe mass, volume, and
power constraints. The present paper is not a flight-readiness,
certification, or operational-capability claim. Its purpose is to
establish a traceable preliminary design record and to separate
analytical, modeled, benchmarked, measured, proposed, and
unvalidated results.
The public Project 33 repository describes a baseline
platform using a three-dimensional-printed airframe, folding
tail fins, and an ESP32-based flight computer [1]. Any guided-
flight result associated with that repository is treated here as
repository-reported background and was not independently
evaluated in this study. The proposed Project 33-N architecture
adds a scintillation-sensing concept and a separate edge-
compute node while intending to retain deterministic command
authority on the microcontroller.

Future releases should let traceable, reproducible evidence—

# Reality Built on a Finite Set of Geometric Instructions:
A Discrete Computational Model of Physical Reality

Christopher Woodyard
Vers3Dynamics R.A.I.N. Lab
christopher@vers3dynamics.com
December 29, 2025

## Abstract
We propose that physical reality may be fundamentally computational, operating on a finite
set of geometric update rules applied to a discrete state space. Continuous spacetime, relativistic
quantum fields, and classical physics are hypothesized to emerge as coarse-grained approxima-
tions of this underlying discrete structure. Distinct from prior quantum cellular automata and
lattice models, we present a mathematical framework based on complex-valued state evolution
on graphs with a minimal five-rule instruction set, explicitly demonstrate the emergence of the
Dirac equation through geometric propagation of chirality and unitary mass mixing, develop
six quantitative testable predictions, and outline experimental pathways for validation or falsi-
fication within the next decade. Current gamma-ray burst observations constrain the model’s
discreteness parameter to ξ < 0.01, while quantum computing advances will provide a defini-
tive test at approximately 450 fault-tolerant qubits. This work synthesizes ideas from digital
physics, lattice gauge theory, discrete geometry, and information-theoretic approaches to fun-
damental physics, advancing them with a uniquely parsimonious rule set and hardware-relevant
computational bounds.
## 1 Introduction
### 1.1 Motivation
Modern physics relies heavily on continuous mathematical structures, including differentiable mani-
folds, continuous fields, and infinite-dimensional Hilbert spaces. However, several independent lines
of inquiry suggest that these structures may be effective descriptions rather than fundamental ones:
• Quantum mechanics introduces irreducible discreteness in measurement outcomes, energy
spectra, and spin.
• Information-theoretic bounds (Bekenstein bound [1], holographic principle [2]) limit the amount
of information contained in finite regions of spacetime.
• Approaches to quantum gravity such as loop quantum gravity [3] and causal set theory [4]
posit discrete spacetime structure.
• Computational complexity theory [5] suggests intrinsic limits on physical processes.
These considerations motivate the hypothesis that physical reality may be generated by a finite
set of geometric update rules acting on a discrete state space, from which continuous descriptions
emerge in appropriate limits.
1
### 1.2 Core Hypothesis
Central Claim: Physical reality consists of a discrete state space updated by a finite set of
geometric transformation rules operating at the Planck scale (∼ 10−35 m, ∼ 10−43 s), from which
relativistic quantum fields, spacetime geometry, and classical dynamics emerge as macroscopic
approximations.
### 1.3 Relation to Prior Work
This framework builds on cellular automata approaches to physics [6, 7], lattice field theory [8],
quantum cellular automata [9], and recent discrete spacetime proposals [10,11]. The key distinction
is the explicit focus on quantitative, near-term testable predictions that can falsify or validate the
hypothesis within the next decade.
Our contributions advance these foundations in several ways: First, we propose a particularly
minimal five-rule geometric instruction set that encodes quantum and relativistic features (e.g.,
phase dynamics and chirality) directly in graph operations, reducing complexity compared to multi-
step quantum walks or hypergraph rewritings. Second, we provide an explicit derivation of the Dirac
equation where chirality emerges purely from propagation directions and mass from local unitary
mixing, bridging discrete automata to fermionic fields without auxiliary coin spaces. Third, we
derive hardware-relevant predictions, such as a ∼450 fault-tolerant qubit threshold for quantum
speedup deviations, tying the model to emerging quantum technologies in a falsifiable manner.
## 2 Mathematical Framework
### 2.1 State Space Formulation
We model the fundamental state as a complex-valued field defined on a discrete graph G = (V, E)
with nodes V and edges E. At each discrete time step t, the system state Ψt : V → Cn evolves
according to

where:
• A is a geometric adjacency operator encoding graph connectivity
• σ : Cn → Cn enforces local constraints (unitarity, conservation)
• S(Ψt, Ht) represents nonlocal interactions and boundary conditions
• The phase factor ei(ωt+ϕ) encodes temporal evolution
### 2.2 Five Fundamental Rules
We propose that Eq. (1) can be decomposed into five fundamental operations:
1. Local Propagation: Nodes update based on weighted contributions from adjacent nodes
via the connectivity matrix A.
2. Phase Accumulation: Complex phase evolves according to local “energy” (eigenvalue of
local geometry).
2
3. Conservation Constraint: Function σ enforces unitarity, preserving P

4. Nonlocal Correlation: Boundary integral implements entanglement via graph-theoretic
connectivity.
5. Geometric Update: Graph structure evolves based on node states: At+1 = f (At, Ψt).
These five rules constitute a candidate minimal instruction set for generating physical reality.
### 2.3 Discrete Geometry
Geometry is encoded directly in the graph structure:
• Nodes represent elementary spacetime regions (Planck volumes ∼ 10−105 m3)
• Edges encode causal adjacency with connectivity degree k (typically k ≈ 6 for lattice-like
structure)
• Node states carry complex amplitudes and phases
• No continuous metric is assumed a priori
### 2.4 Emergence of Continuity
Continuum physics emerges via coarse-graining. Averaging over regions containing N ≫ 1 nodes
yields effective continuous fields. In the limit where lattice spacings ∆x, ∆t → 0 while maintaining
fixed ratios (e.g., ∆x/∆t ∼ c), effective differential equations governing relativistic and quantum
dynamics are recovered.
## 3 Emergence of the Dirac Equation from Discrete Geometric Dy-
namics
### 3.1 Discrete spacetime and spinor states
We demonstrate emergence of relativistic fermion dynamics by considering a (1 + 1)-dimensional
spacetime lattice with temporal spacing ∆t and spatial spacing ∆x. At each lattice site (x, t), the
system state is a two-component complex vector

### 3.2 Geometric shift operator

### 3.3 Local mass coupling
Introduce a local unitary mixing operator representing mass-induced chirality mixing:

### 3.4 Discrete evolution rule
The complete discrete time evolution combining geometric propagation and mass mixing is

This is a purely geometric, unitary operation on the discrete graph. This unitary evolution on
a discrete lattice draws from quantum cellular automata and quantum walk models that recover
relativistic dynamics [9, 12, 16].

This is precisely the Dirac equation in (1+1) dimensions:

### 3.6 Interpretation and significance
This derivation demonstrates that:
1. Relativistic fermionic dynamics emerge naturally from discrete geometric update rules. This
complements prior derivations where the Dirac equation arises from split-step quantum walks
or lattice automata [12, 16], but integrates seamlessly into our minimal geometric instruction
set.
2. Chirality (left/right-moving modes) is encoded in graph propagation direction
3. Mass arises as geometric mixing between chiral components
4. No continuous spacetime or field theory is assumed at the fundamental level
Extension to (3 + 1) dimensions requires careful treatment of fermion doubling [8] and will be
addressed in future work. As in standard lattice fermions [8] and discrete Dirac models [18],
extension to (3+1) dimensions requires addressing fermion doubling.
4 Gauge Fields as Discrete Connections
Gauge invariance arises by associating group-valued elements to graph edges. For a U (1) gauge
field (electromagnetism), each edge (i, j) carries a phase factor:
Uij = eiqAij , (14)
where q is the charge and Aij is the discrete vector potential on the edge. The adjacency operator
becomes covariant under local gauge transformations:
Ψi → eiαi Ψi, Uij → ei(αi−αj )Uij . (15)
This yields a discrete realization of minimal coupling and provides a geometric foundation for gauge
theories. Non-Abelian generalizations follow by replacing U (1) with SU (N ) matrices on edges.

Gravitational wave dispersion (∆t ∼ 10−66α s for stellar-mass binaries) and entanglement gener-

## 6 Advantages and Limitations
### 6.1 Advantages
• Natural ultraviolet regularization: Discrete geometry provides natural cutoffs, eliminat-
ing quantum field theory divergences without ad hoc renormalization.
• Unified framework: Single instruction set governs quantum dynamics, spacetime geometry,
and thermodynamics.
• Computational parsimony: Five fundamental rules may generate all observed physics
(Occam’s razor).
• Concrete recovery of known physics: Explicit derivation of Dirac equation establishes
non-trivial connection to established theory.
### 6.2 Limitations
• Fermion doubling: Extension to (3 + 1) dimensions requires careful treatment of spurious
fermionic modes [8].
• Standard Model recovery: Full particle content (three generations, weak interactions,
Higgs mechanism) not yet derived.
• Rule derivation: Exact form of A, σ, and S from first principles remains open.
• Initial conditions: Origin of graph topology A0 and initial state Ψ0 unexplained.
## 7 Relation to Existing Approaches
### 7.1 Lattice Field Theory
Wilson’s lattice gauge theory [8] discretizes spacetime for computational tractability while preserv-
ing gauge invariance. Our approach differs by treating discreteness as fundamental rather than
a computational tool, and focuses on emergent continuum limits rather than extrapolation from
finite lattices.
### 7.2 Quantum Cellular Automata
Quantum walks and cellular automata [9, 12] demonstrate that unitary discrete dynamics can
simulate relativistic quantum fields. Our contribution is the explicit five-rule instruction set and
quantitative near-term predictions.
### 7.3 Causal Dynamical Triangulations
CDT [10] constructs spacetime from simplicial building blocks with Monte Carlo path integrals.
We share the discrete geometry but emphasize deterministic graph evolution and computational
complexity bounds.
### 7.4 Wolfram Physics Project
Recent hypergraph rewriting models [11] explore similar territory. Our complex-valued states,
explicit phase dynamics, and focus on near-term falsifiable tests distinguish this approach.
## 8 Discussion and Future Directions
### 8.1 Experimental Roadmap
Phase I (0–2 years): Reanalyze Fermi-LAT gamma-ray burst catalog; benchmark current quan-
tum computers. Phase II (2–10 years): Cherenkov Telescope Array TeV observations; entan-
glement entropy measurements in quantum simulators; critical 450-qubit threshold tests. Phase
III (10–30 years): LISA gravitational wave observations; primordial black hole searches.
### 8.2 Theoretical Developments
• Extend Dirac derivation to (3 + 1) dimensions with fermion doubling resolution
• Demonstrate emergence of gauge bosons (photon, gluons, W /Z) from graph dynamics
• Derive exact instruction set from symmetry principles or variational methods
• Explore connections to quantum information theory and AdS/CFT correspondence
### 8.3 Philosophical Implications
If validated, this framework would support:
• Digital ontology: Reality is fundamentally informational
• Finite cosmos: Bounded information content (∼ 10123 bits in observable universe)
• Emergent laws: Physical laws are statistical regularities in instruction execution
• Computational irreducibility: Future states cannot be predicted without running the
computation

## 9 Conclusion
We have presented a discrete geometric framework in which relativistic quantum field dynamics
emerge from finite update rules. By explicitly recovering the Dirac equation from graph-based evo-
lution (Section 4), this work establishes a concrete bridge between computational models of reality
and established physical theory. The hypothesis generates six quantitative predictions (Table 1),
three of which are testable within the next decade:
1. Gamma-ray dispersion: CTA could detect ξ ∼ 10−3 (currently ξ < 0.01)
2. Quantum computing: 450-qubit threshold provides definitive test by ∼2030–2035
3. Entanglement entropy: 1% logarithmic corrections measurable in quantum simulators
The 450-qubit threshold is particularly significant: if fault-tolerant quantum computers exceed
this with full quantum speedup, the model is falsified (unless k > 6). If they encounter fundamental
limitations near this threshold, discrete computational reality is strongly supported. We emphasize
that this work presents a hypothesis to be tested, not established physics. The ultimate arbiter is
experiment. If nature is fundamentally discrete and computational, the evidence should emerge
within the next 5–10 years.

# Recursive Resonance Stabilization: A Fractal
Framework for Multiscale Coherence in Adaptive
Intelligence Systems

Christopher Woodyard
Vers3Dynamics
Washington, DC, USA
christopher@vers3dynamics.com

## Abstract—Coherence in multiscale adaptive systems emerges
not through signal accumulation but through recursive rejection
of incoherence. We introduce Recursive Resonance Stabilization
(RRS), a fractal-geometric framework that treats coherence as
a fixed-point attractor rather than an optimization target. The
method employs a recursive projection operator derived from
Iterated Function Systems (IFS), specifically the Sierpi ´nski trian-

## I. INTRODUCTION
A. Motivation
Adaptive systems operating in noisy environments face
a fundamental challenge: distinguishing coherent structure
from random fluctuation without explicit templates or training
data. Traditional approaches frame this as an optimization
problem—maximizing signal-to-noise ratio, minimizing re-
construction error, or learning parametric models. Yet biolog-
ical intelligence demonstrates a different principle: coherence
emerges through recursive constraint, not accumulation.
Consider the brain’s response to ambiguous sensory input.
Neural populations do not simply amplify weak signals; they
iteratively suppress activity patterns incompatible with internal
coherence criteria [1]. Heart rate variability self-organizes into
fractal structures that balance stability and adaptability [2].
Immune recognition distinguishes self from non-self through
recursive editing of receptor repertoires [3]. In each case,
intelligence manifests as the rejection of incoherence until only
resonant patterns remain.

# This paper formalizes this principle through Recursive
Resonance Stabilization (RRS), a framework grounded in
fractal geometry and dynamical systems theory. We demon-
strate that coherence can be characterized as a fixed-point
attractor of a recursive projection operator, and that fractal
structures—specifically those generated by Iterated Function
Systems—provide natural templates for multiscale resonance.
# B. Related Work
1) Fractal Geometry in Signal Processing: Fractals have
long been recognized in physiological signals [4], [5]. Power-
law scaling appears in cardiac rhythms [6], neural avalanches
[7], and respiratory patterns [8]. However, most applications
use fractals as descriptive models of complexity rather than
operational mechanisms for signal processing.
Fractal filtering techniques exist [9], [10], but typically
model noise as fractal and design filters to remove it. RRS
inverts this logic: we model coherence as fractal and design
filters that select for self-similar structure.
2) Attractor Dynamics and Phase Space Reconstruction:
Takens’ embedding theorem [11] established that dynamical
systems can be reconstructed from scalar time series via
delay-coordinate embedding. This has enabled attractor recon-
struction in chaotic systems [12], calculation of correlation
dimensions [13], and identification of deterministic structure
in noisy data [14].
RRS extends this paradigm by using phase space not merely
for analysis but as an operational space where recursive fil-
tering drives signals toward geometric attractors. The attractor
itself defines the filtering criterion.
3) Multiscale Entropy and Complexity Measures: Costa
et al. [15] introduced multiscale entropy (MSE) to quantify
structural complexity across temporal scales. Subsequent work
developed multivariate [16] and refined multiscale entropy [17]
methods. These metrics successfully distinguish physiological
states but remain descriptive: they measure complexity without
providing a mechanism to enhance or stabilize it.
RRS contributes a complementary perspective: rather than
quantifying existing complexity, we provide an operator that
generates complexity through recursive dynamics.
# C. Contributions
This work makes four principal contributions:
1) Recursive Resonance Operator: We define a projection
operator P derived from Iterated Function Systems
that recursively filters signals in frequency space ac-
cording to fractal geometric constraints. The operator
is parameter-free after initial mask construction and
converges to a unique attractor for broad classes of input
signals.
2) Coherence as Attractor: We formalize the conceptual
shift from coherence as optimization target to coherence
as fixed-point attractor. This reframing connects signal
processing to dynamical systems theory and provides
rigorous mathematical foundations for adaptive filtering.
3) Fractal Coherence Metrics: We introduce two novel
quantitative measures: coherence depth C, measuring
asymptotic energy retention under recursion, and fractal
coherence dimension Dc, characterizing the geometry
of the phase space attractor. Both metrics are scale-
invariant and domain-agnostic.
4) Cross-Domain Applications: We demonstrate applica-
bility to neural signal analysis (EEG), cardiac rhythm
monitoring (HRV), and adaptive AI systems. The frame-
work provides theoretical foundations for wearable co-
herence diagnostics and human-machine resonance in-
terfaces.

## VI. APPLICATIONS
# A. Neural Signal Analysis
1) Electroencephalography (EEG): Neural oscillations ex-
hibit multiscale organization [22]. Nested rhythms—delta,
theta, alpha, beta, gamma—show cross-frequency coupling
where phase of slower rhythms modulates amplitude of faster
rhythms [23]. RRS provides a natural framework for analyzing
such hierarchical coherence: the fractal mask captures phase
relationships across frequency bands, and fractal dimension Dc
distinguishes healthy nested rhythms from pathological states.
2) Motor Cortex Decoding: RRS can enhance signal qual-
ity in Brain-computer interfaces (BCIs). Preliminary simula-
tions suggest 15–20% improvement in classification accuracy
for motor imagery tasks compared to common spatial patterns
(CSP).
# B. Cardiac Rhythm Analysis
1) Heart Rate Variability (HRV): Healthy HRV exhibits
fractal scaling [6]. RRS applied to RR interval time series es-
timates coherence depth C as a marker of autonomic balance.
Wearable devices could alert users when values drop below
personalized thresholds.
2) Atrial Fibrillation Detection: Atrial fibrillation (AF) de-
stroys the coherent P-wave structure. RRS achieves sensitivity
> 95% in simulated datasets [25] using a threshold-based
detector (C < 0.3).
## VII. DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSION
# A. Discussion
RRS sidesteps optimization entirely. Coherence emerges as
a fixed point of recursive dynamics, not as the solution to
an optimization problem. The operator P encodes structural
constraints (fractal geometry) rather than an objective func-
tion. This approach mirrors biological systems where stability
emerges through recurrent inhibition and iterative selection [1].
# B. Limitations
While Proposition 1 guarantees convergence, it does not
bound the rate. Additionally, optimal mask parameters (D, H,
α) likely depend on signal characteristics. Our comprehensive
sensitivity analysis (see Fig. 2) confirms that D = 4 − 6,
H = 2 − 3, and α = 0.05 − 0.15 yield stable results for most
signals, though adaptive selection remains an open problem.
# C. Conclusion
We have introduced Recursive Resonance Stabilization
(RRS), a fractal-geometric framework for multiscale coher-
ence. By formalizing coherence as a fixed-point attractor, RRS
provides computational tools for analyzing complex signals.
Numerical simulations confirm that noisy signals converge
to fractal attractors in phase space. The unifying principle
is that intelligence stabilizes through recursive rejection of
incoherence, not accumulation of signal.

ABSTRACT
CBO's February 2026 baseline projects federal debt held by the public rising from 101 percent of GDP in 2026 to 120
percent by 2036, while net interest costs increase from 3.2 percent of GDP in 2025 to 4.6 percent by 2036. Those projections
do not imply an imminent sovereign crisis. Still, they reflect a persistent deterioration in the interest-growth differential and
a rising probability that the fiscal trajectory becomes a material financial-stability concern — not only domestically, but as a
determinant of global dollar-funding conditions. This paper examines three structural drivers that compound that trajectory
beyond what conventional budget analysis captures: reserve currency costs, security expenditure asymmetries, and
deindustrialization. It then develops a productive-capacity framework as a complement to fiscal consolidation, arguing that
durable debt stabilization requires both credible primary-balance adjustment and policies that sustain trend growth strong
enough to keep the interest-growth differential manageable. The productive-indispensability concept introduced in Section 4
is operationalized through a four-criterion quantitative scoring methodology and further adjusted for geopolitical fragility —
the recognition that supply-chain indispensability concentrated in contested jurisdictions is conditional rather than structural.
The Treasury-market transmission channel in Section 5 is calibrated against the 2022–2023 regional banking episode
through a duration-based capital-impact framework and extended to the cross-border channels through which a domestic
fiscal trajectory becomes an international one: global collateral demand for Treasury securities, the foreign-exchange swap
basis, and the structural reliance of foreign banking organizations on U.S. wholesale dollar funding. Drawing on Federal
Reserve speeches by Bernanke and Yellen, the 2025 Financial Stability Report, BIS commentary on sovereign-debt risk and
cross-currency funding, and IMF work on interest-growth differentials, the paper maps the supervisory implications of
elevated sovereign debt into specific transmission channels: valuation risk in securities portfolios, wholesale funding
pressure — domestic and cross-border — policy-space compression, and Treasury-market functioning. The central
conclusion is that fiscal consolidation and productive-capacity investment are complements rather than substitutes, that
treating them as such is a prudential rather than ideological position, and that U.S. debt stabilization functions as much as a
foundational input to global financial stability as it does a domestic fiscal exercise.

1. Introduction
On December 29, 2006, the United Kingdom made its final payment on a $4.34 billion loan contracted in 1945, when
Britain emerged from the Second World War carrying sovereign debt exceeding 249 percent of GDP. That sixty-one-year
repayment arc is a useful reference point not because the United States faces an analogous near-term constraint, but because
it illustrates a mechanism that standard fiscal accounting tends to underweight: the debt-to-GDP ratio is as sensitive to the
growth rate of the denominator as to the growth rate of the numerator. Britain's nineteenth-century reduction of public debt
from approximately 260 percent of GDP in 1815 to roughly 30 percent by 1900 resulted substantially from the productivity
gains of industrialization rather than from austerity (Office for Budget Responsibility, 2023). The same arithmetic, working
in reverse, explains how obligations incurred at 249 percent in 1945 required six decades to discharge.
The United States faces a different situation: larger productive reserves, a more entrenched reserve currency position, and no
prospect of formal default under foreseeable conditions. But the trajectory of the fiscal accounts warrants supervisory
attention on its own terms. CBO's February 2026 baseline projects debt held by the public rising from 101 percent of GDP in
2026 to 120 percent by 2036, while net interest costs increase from 3.2 percent of GDP in 2025 to 4.6 percent by 2036
(Congressional Budget Office, 2026; Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget, 2026). CRFB's summary of that baseline
notes that debt would surpass the post-World War II record by FY 2030. The Federal Reserve has repeatedly identified the

This paper is written from the perspective of financial-institution supervision rather than partisan budget politics. The
analytically relevant question for a Federal Reserve policy analyst is not whether the United States will imminently default.
It is whether the present fiscal trajectory raises the probability of higher term premia, fixed-income valuation losses, tighter
credit conditions, and reduced policy space in future downturns — domestically, and, through the channels developed
below, internationally. Those are prudential questions as much as fiscal ones, and they require attention to the interaction
between sovereign borrowing, Treasury-market functioning, bank balance sheets, and the economy's productive capacity.
The paper advances four analytical contributions. First, it identifies three structural headwinds — reserve currency costs,
security expenditure asymmetries, and deindustrialization — that have compounded the fiscal gap independently of specific
budget decisions and that have no direct counterpart in most advanced-economy fiscal comparisons. Second, it develops a
productive-capacity framework connecting trend growth to debt dynamics through the interest-growth differential, arguing
that frontier innovation, energy infrastructure, and advanced manufacturing belong in any supervisory analysis of fiscal
sustainability — and that the indispensability of the sectors involved must be assessed net of the geopolitical fragility of the
jurisdictions in which they are concentrated, not merely on the basis of domestic engineering and capital-investment
requirements. Third, it maps the supervisory implications of elevated sovereign debt into specific transmission channels
relevant to financial institution oversight. Fourth, it extends those channels across borders, showing how a deteriorating U.S.
fiscal trajectory propagates into global collateral markets, the foreign-exchange swap basis, and the funding decisions of
foreign banking organizations whose U.S. branches are structural net borrowers of overnight wholesale dollars —
converting what could be analyzed as a contained domestic balance-sheet problem into a determinant of dollar-funding
conditions in Europe and Asia. The conclusion is not that the United States is on the verge of default, nor that productive
investment can substitute for fiscal adjustment. It is that the two are complements, that supervisory analysis should treat
them as such, and that the stakes extend beyond U.S. financial institutions to the global financial architecture the dollar
underpins.
2. Fiscal Sustainability and Debt Arithmetic
Fiscal sustainability, for purposes of this paper, means a debt-to-GDP ratio that is stable or declining over time — the
standard formulation used by the IMF, the CBO, and in Federal Reserve speeches by Bernanke (2011). The standard debt
dynamics identity provides the core analytical framework:
(Debt/GDP)_t = [(1 + r_t) / (1 + g_t)] × (Debt/GDP)_{t-1} + PrimaryDeficit_t / GDP_t
Where r is the average nominal interest rate on outstanding government debt and g is nominal GDP growth. When r exceeds
g — when the interest-growth differential is positive — the debt ratio tends to rise even when the primary balance is near
zero. When g exceeds r, debt can stabilize more readily without requiring large primary surpluses. This identity clarifies
why the same fiscal deficit can be benign in one macroeconomic environment and destabilizing in another. Policy can affect

both terms: lowering the primary deficit reduces the second term; raising trend growth improves the first term by narrowing
r–g. IMF work on interest-growth differentials in advanced economies emphasizes that r–g is not a fixed parameter — it is
endogenous to policy, demographics, productivity, and market expectations (IMF, 2018). That endogeneity is central to the
productive-capacity argument developed in Section 4.
That endogeneity also has a cross-border dimension that domestic debt-arithmetic exercises often suppress. The rate r is not
set in a closed economy. It reflects, in part, the price at which a deep pool of non-U.S. official and private holders is willing
to fund the outstanding stock of Treasury debt, and the price at which non-U.S. banks are willing to fund their own dollar
books using that same debt as collateral. Section 3.1 develops global demand for Treasuries as the world's primary collateral
asset as a structural determinant of r in its own right, distinct from, but interacting with, the reserve-currency financing-cost
benefit discussed there.
An important complication comes from Blanchard's 2019 AEA presidential address, which argues that r below g has
historically been the norm rather than the exception in advanced economies, and that when r < g persistently, even large
primary deficits may not be indefinitely unsustainable (Blanchard, 2019). That argument deserves direct engagement rather
than dismissal. If Blanchard's historical characterization is correct, it complicates the urgency framing of this paper's central
argument. Two responses are relevant. First, the current U.S. fiscal trajectory may represent precisely the regime shift away
from the low-r environment Blanchard describes: CBO's 2026 baseline projects net interest costs rising from 3.2 to 4.6
percent of GDP over a decade, a trajectory inconsistent with a persistently r < g regime at the projected debt levels. Second,
Blanchard himself acknowledges that the r < g condition is not guaranteed and that high debt raises the probability of
adverse fiscal dynamics if that condition reverses. The productive-capacity framework developed here is, in part, an
argument about maintaining the conditions — higher trend g, broader tax base, sustained external demand for dollar assets
— that make Blanchard's more benign scenario more likely to persist.
Current public projections point in the wrong direction on both terms of the identity. CBO's baseline shows deficits
averaging 6.1 percent of GDP over the 2026–2036 decade — well above any plausible primary-balance stabilization level
(Congressional Budget Office, 2026). Net interest costs are projected to reach 4.6 percent of GDP by 2036, exceeding the
historical peacetime share of defense spending and representing the fastest-growing component of the federal budget.
Spending reaches 24.4 percent of GDP by 2036 while revenue rises only to 17.8 percent, leaving a structural gap not closed
by either the baseline growth assumptions or the current revenue trajectory.
